title: Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. v. Haeger
lead: Goodyear’s concealed tire tests justified sanctions, but civil fee shifting had to compensate for expenses caused by the misconduct. The Supreme Court required but-for causation and left a waiver question for remand.

actors.name: Leroy, Donna, Barry and Suzanne Haeger
actors.role: Motorhome occupants suing over an alleged tire failure

actors.name: Goodyear Tire & Rubber Company
actors.role: Tire manufacturer sanctioned for bad-faith discovery conduct

actors.name: Justice Kagan
actors.role: Author of the unanimous opinion for eight participating Justices

proceedings: After settlement, district court awarded approximately $2.7 million in inherent-power sanctions and a contingent $2 million alternative.
Ninth Circuit affirmed the larger award over Judge Watford’s dissent.
Supreme Court reversed and remanded for waiver determination and, absent waiver, a new causation assessment.
limits: The Supreme Court did not decide the accident’s cause, affirm the $2 million alternative, or eliminate all sanctions.
The separately briefed 2018 remand is not the 2017 holding. Settlement was not held categorically to eliminate Rule 37 authority.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The tests emerge after settlement
sections.cue: Begin with the accident allegations and discovery failure.
paragraphs: Leroy, Donna, Barry and Suzanne Haeger sued Goodyear Tire & Rubber Company after their motorhome left the road and overturned. They alleged that a G159 tire failed because it could not withstand heat generated by highway-speed motorhome use. They also sued the motorhome and chassis manufacturers. The Supreme Court’s later sanctions ruling did not establish that alleged accident cause.

For years, the Haegers requested internal G159 testing data and encountered slow, uninformative responses and disputes requiring judicial intervention. The case settled for an undisclosed amount shortly before trial. Months later, their lawyer learned from a newspaper report that Goodyear had produced relevant heat tests in another lawsuit. Those tests showed unusual heating between fifty-five and sixty-five miles per hour. Goodyear acknowledged withholding them here despite repeated requests for all testing data.

The Haegers moved for sanctions. The district court found years of bad faith by Goodyear and its lawyers aimed at frustrating a merits resolution. Goodyear did not challenge that assessment in the Supreme Court. Settlement prevented the default judgment the trial judge otherwise wanted, so the court used its inherent authority to award litigation fees and costs.

sections.title: The judge awards all later fees and a smaller alternative
sections.cue: Explain the two amounts and the appellate disagreement.
paragraphs: The district court awarded approximately $2.7 million, covering all fees and costs from Goodyear’s first dishonest discovery response forward. It recognized the ordinary causal requirement but believed sufficiently egregious conduct justified shifting even unrelated expenses. It also thought timely disclosure probably would have produced substantially earlier settlement, while expressing uncertainty.

Anticipating a stricter appellate requirement, the judge made a contingent $2 million award. Based on Goodyear’s estimates, it subtracted roughly $700,000 attributable to other defendants and medical damages. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the larger award because the expenses were incurred while Goodyear acted in bad faith. Judge Watford dissented: simultaneous timing was not causation, and Goodyear retained plausible defenses even with full disclosure.

The Supreme Court considered whether an inherent-power fee sanction imposed through civil procedures could exceed the expenses caused by misconduct. The parties largely agreed on the general standard but disputed its application and whether either award could survive.

sections.title: Civil reimbursement must follow the harm caused
sections.cue: Explain the but-for rule and permissible estimation.
paragraphs: Justice Kagan wrote for all eight participating Justices. Federal courts possess inherent power to manage litigation and sanction bad-faith abuse, including reimbursement of an opponent’s legal expenses. Through ordinary civil procedures, however, that award must compensate rather than punish. Punishment requires criminal procedural protections, including the appropriate proof standard. Coercive sanctions designed to secure compliance were not at issue.

Drawing on Fox v. Vice, an earlier fee-allocation decision, the Court required expenses that the innocent party would not have incurred but for the misconduct. Work that proper disclosure would not have avoided—such as an independently necessary deposition or motion—could not be shifted merely to punish. Rule-based and statutory sanctions similarly connect expenses to offending conduct.

Exact accounting was unnecessary. A judge familiar with the litigation could estimate time, allocate percentages, or attribute an entire expenditure category to misconduct, with substantial appellate deference. That flexibility concerned calculation, not elimination of causation.

All fees could qualify in an exceptional case under the same rule: a lawsuit initiated in bad faith might cause every defense expense, an entire scheme to defeat a valid claim might cause all litigation costs, or a supported finding that proper disclosure would have produced settlement at a particular point might justify every later fee. Those were applications of but-for causation, not exceptions for especially egregious behavior.

sections.title: The record does not sustain the comprehensive award
sections.cue: Apply causation without deciding tire liability.
paragraphs: The district court expressly substituted severity for causation, and the Ninth Circuit used the period of bad faith as its boundary. Neither found each shifted expense incurred because of, and solely because of, the misconduct. Temporal overlap could not support the $2.7 million award.

The Haegers argued that timely disclosure would have ended the case. The Court declined to make that finding. The district court said only that settlement probably would have occurred much earlier, not immediately after disclosure should have occurred. Goodyear still could contend that a tire used for more than 40,000 miles failed from road debris; in another G159 case, it disclosed the tests and still went to trial. Those were plausible litigation positions, not findings that debris caused this accident.

The alternative award also acknowledged roughly $700,000 for other defendants and medical damages that would have been litigated anyway. The Haegers gave no concrete reason to disregard that distinction. At least those expenses could not enter the full award.

sections.title: Waiver determines the next step for the smaller award
sections.cue: Finish at the Supreme Court’s actual stopping point.
paragraphs: Ordinarily, the sparse explanation for the contingent $2 million award would also require recalculation. But the Haegers argued that Goodyear waived further challenge by submitting that only about $700,000 would have been incurred regardless of misconduct. The Ninth Circuit had not addressed waiver, and the Supreme Court would not decide it first.

On April 18, 2017, the Court reversed and remanded. If waiver existed, the contingent award could end the dispute; otherwise, the district court had to reassess fees under but-for causation. The Court neither approved $2 million itself nor erased every sanction. Justice Gorsuch did not participate, and there were no separate Supreme Court opinions.

The subsequent 2018 district-court decision is a separate remand stage. Nor did this ruling establish that settlement invariably disables Rule 37 sanctions: the opinion explained settlement’s effect on default judgment and recounted the district court’s view that Rule 11 and 28 U.S.C. § 1927 did not reach all the misconduct.

sources.pinpoint: 581 U.S. at 105 n. 2, 114–115; assigned discussion at 976–977
